title: Compute:Arena / Measuring Local Inference Across Models, Quants, Chips, and Runtimes
gist: Basecompute open-sourced Compute:Arena, a public CLI benchmark and leaderboard that measures local LLM inference performance across the interacting dimensions of model, quantization, chip, and runtime, using signed, hash-verified, offline-first reports that transparently disclose the methodology's own limits.

themes.theme: The measurement problem in local inference

insights.claim: Local inference performance is determined by the interaction of model, quantization format, chip, and runtime together, so no single spec sheet value reliably predicts real-world throughput.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating on-device AI hardware or software claims should discount vendor-supplied spec comparisons and look for cross-runtime, cross-quant empirical benchmarks instead.
insights.quote: Local inference performance is a four-dimensional problem.

insights.claim: The same Llama weights produce three materially different, non-interchangeable performance measurements depending on combination: Q4_K_M via llama.cpp on an Apple M4 Pro, the same weights in MLX's 4-bit format on the same M4 Pro chip, and the equivalent GGUF running on an Nvidia GB10 via CUDA.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: Chip vendors' (Apple, Nvidia) inference-speed marketing claims for a given model are not portable across quantization format or runtime, so buyers should demand runtime-matched benchmarks before sizing hardware purchases.
insights.quote: Llama in Q4_K_M through llama.cpp on an M4 Pro, the same weights in MLX's 4-bit format on the same chip, and the same GGUF on a GB10 with CUDA are three different measurements, and none of them is predictable from a spec sheet.

insights.claim: Memory bandwidth, quantization scheme, and runtime scheduling interact in ways that make empirical measurement the only reliable way to know local inference performance, rather than inferring it from any one of those factors alone.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: Reinforces that on-device AI performance claims are an empirical, testable market rather than a spec-driven one, favoring tools/platforms that supply real measurement data.

insights.claim: Compute:Arena's leaderboard identifies every benchmark entry precisely: the model file by SHA-256 hash, the quantization namespaced by format (so BaseRT's Q4 and GGUF's Q4_K_M are tracked as distinct variants rather than conflated), the chip with normalized naming (while preserving the runtime's original raw value), and the runtime executable itself also hashed.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: This level of identity precision is what makes cross-vendor local-inference benchmarks trustworthy and comparable, a bar most informal community benchmarks don't meet.
insights.locator: Compute:Arena is a public leaderboard and CLI

insights.claim: Each Compute:Arena submission runs an identical, standardized sweep -- prefill throughput measured across prompt sizes from 128 to 16,384 tokens, plus decode throughput over 128 tokens, with warmups and three recorded repetitions -- so any two leaderboard entries are directly comparable at every workload size.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: A standardized, granular prefill/decode sweep lets buyers match hardware choice to their actual workload's prompt-length profile rather than a single headline tokens/sec number.
insights.locator: What gets measured is prefill throughput swept from 128 to 16384 tokens

insights.claim: Compute:Arena supports exactly two runtimes through one adapter interface -- BaseRT for .base bundles and stock llama.cpp's llama-bench for .gguf files -- with its llama.cpp picker able to search Hugging Face directly for models to benchmark.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: Narrow initial runtime coverage signals an early-stage tool; watch whether the promised expansion to more runtimes materializes as a signal of ecosystem traction.

themes.theme: Trust and integrity design of the benchmark

insights.claim: Compute:Arena runs and verifies benchmarks entirely offline and uploads nothing until the user logs in, reviews the exact JSON payload that will become public, and explicitly submits it -- a consent-first design intended to lower the barrier to community contribution of benchmark data from machines basecompute doesn't own.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: This privacy-preserving submission flow is a deliberate growth lever for crowdsourcing a hardware benchmark dataset that would otherwise be expensive for a single company to generate.

insights.claim: Each signed benchmark report captures raw per-repetition token counts and timings, model and executable file hashes taken both before and after the run (so a swapped file aborts signing), resolved chip identity with its detection source, and automatic telemetry -- temperature sensors, power state, memory pressure, swap, and GPU snapshots -- so thermal throttling conditions are disclosed in the data rather than averaged away.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: Exposing thermal/power telemetry alongside throughput numbers lets analysts distinguish sustained performance from short-burst benchmark scores, a common gap in chip marketing.

insights.claim: basecompute pins Compute:Arena's model downloads to immutable Hugging Face revisions and checks them against published LFS hashes, preventing silent model drift between the time a benchmark is run and when it's reviewed.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: Supply-chain integrity controls like immutable revision pinning are a differentiator for benchmark credibility versus ad hoc community numbers.
insights.locator: Model downloads are pinned to immutable Hugging Face revisions

insights.claim: basecompute explicitly discloses the limits of its own trust model: the Ed25519 signature on a report only proves the data hasn't changed since signing, not that the reporting machine's telemetry was truthful, and the company makes no claim of exact cross-runtime equivalence since llama-bench and the BaseRT harness differ in workload order and warmup behavior.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: This candor about benchmark limitations is itself a credibility signal worth noting when assessing whether to trust the leaderboard for procurement decisions -- but it also means results still can't fully rule out gaming.
insights.quote: The Ed25519 signature proves a report hasn't changed since it was signed, not that the machine told the truth.

insights.claim: Compute:Arena began as basecompute's internal harness for tracking chip and model performance over time and was open-sourced under Apache-2.0 on GitHub specifically to source benchmark measurements from machines the company itself doesn't own.
insights.speaker: Lukas Wesemann
insights.so_what: Open-sourcing an internal tool to crowdsource data is a low-cost way for a small local-inference infra vendor (basecompute, also behind BaseRT) to build a proprietary dataset and community mindshare ahead of monetizing BaseRT or related products.
insights.quote: It started as the harness we used internally to track chip and model performance over time. We've open sourced it so the measurements can come from more machines than we own.
